summary:
Puerto Rico is a United States territory, and the United States federal framework applies on the island in full: federal statutes, executive orders and agency procedure govern entry, documents, federally funded care and federal custody. Puerto Rico's own legislation does not soften that framework, and in the area of trans medical care it sharpens it.

United States travel documents record sex assigned at birth, and Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, eliminated the X marker, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents may present a marker that does not match their appearance at inspection. Entry scrutiny is tightened further for one category of traveller: in February 2025 the United States State Department announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

Consensual private sexual activity between adults is not criminalised in Puerto Rico. The Puerto Rico Supreme Court upheld the territory's sodomy ban in 2002; the United States Supreme Court's Lawrence v. Texas ruling in 2003 invalidated state and territorial sodomy statutes covering consensual private acts, and Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute.

In July 2025 Puerto Rico enacted Ley Núm. 63 de 2025, which bars gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, withdraws public funding for that care, and punishes violations with a fixed 15-year prison term, a $50,000 fine per violation for legal persons, and permanent loss of medical licences for professionals. Article 4 of the law directs the prohibition at medical institutions and health professionals, forbidding surgical interventions or medication treatments that alter sex biology under the pretext of gender transition or as part of gender-dysphoria treatment. Article 3 defines the banned chemical and surgical practice more broadly than the operative clause: it expressly names the use of puberty blockers and sex hormones, including androgen blockers, oestrogen, progesterone or testosterone, when used to treat gender dysphoria, and sets the age of the protected class at under 21.

The drafting leaves an unresolved gap between a definition framed around patient use and an operative clause that restricts only providers, while Article 6 penalises any person who violates the law. Under ordinary criminal-law principles a successful prosecution of a visiting under-21 trans person for using their own lawfully prescribed hormones, or of a parent accompanying them, would almost certainly fail, and no test case had resolved the question at the time of writing. What the ambiguity produces instead is exposure to questioning, detention or investigation by hostile officials, with the answer arriving only after the fact. For an under-21 trans traveller the practical reading is that carrying and using prescribed hormone treatment in Puerto Rico sits inside the law's literal definition of a banned practice, and that enforcement risk is harassment-shaped rather than conviction-shaped.

The law was pushed through non-public hearings and is written with deliberate vagueness, so doctors and affirming parents who facilitate hormone treatment or top surgery risk prosecution, a reach that extends to the accompanying parents of a travelling trans teenager. It mandates campaigns by the Education and Health departments on the risks of trans-affirming care. Health Secretary Víctor Ramos Parés proposed amendments that would have allowed puberty blockers and the continuation of existing hormone treatment, but the text as enacted stands as the most restrictive care law in any United States jurisdiction according to the report documenting it. The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court.

Opposition to the measure was registered across the island's professional bodies before signature. The ACLU of Puerto Rico urged Governor Jenniffer González Colón to veto Senate Bill 350, stating that it criminalizes doctors and parents and creates two distinct categories of children divided by whether identity aligns with sex assigned at birth. The Puerto Rico College of Physicians and Surgeons, the Puerto Rico Psychology Association, the College of Social Work Professionals, the Puerto Rican Association of Professional Counseling, the Puerto Rico Bar Association and the LGBTQ+ Federation of Puerto Rico all opposed it.

Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the United States federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. The first hate crime charges in Puerto Rico's history were brought in 2020, after Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged in the murder of two transgender women on 22 April 2020; Bonilla confessed to the killings. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island.

Anti-discrimination coverage remains partial. The 2013 law that passed (Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013) was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities, housing, transit and business transactions are not covered by it. An earlier bill, House Bill 1725, passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 with wider coverage but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved.

Marriage recognition for same-sex couples in Puerto Rico was won through federal court rather than local statute. The challenge filed in March 2014, the Ada Conde Vidal case, drew intervention from Lambda Legal and Puerto Rico Para Todas, and in June 2014 four couples joined as plaintiffs, among them a former National Guard member and two couples already married in Canada in 2007 and New York in 2012.

Under Executive Order 14168, which directs United States federal agencies to recognise only two sexes, the Bureau of Prisons houses transgender inmates by sex assigned at birth rather than asserted gender identity, a rule that governs any federal custody in Puerto Rico. The ACLU said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting how many transgender people it holds. Advocates say the order contravenes the Prison Rape Elimination Act requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided by individual safety assessment.
tangentialFactors:
Puerto Rico's legislature has repeatedly been the site of contested LGB and trans-adjacent bills whose outcomes cut in both directions. In 2019 the pro-statehood New Progressive Party caucus in the House of Representatives blocked a floor vote on Senate Bill 1000, which would have banned conversion therapy for minors, and the bill died despite Senate passage and the governor's support; Senator Zoe Laboy, a co-sponsor, dissented publicly.

The same year Governor Ricardo Rosselló announced Senate Bills 1253 and 1254, pairing a religious-freedom measure with a conversion-therapy ban carrying a pastoral exemption for clergy. LGBT council president Johanne Velez Garcia and allies said the pairing would open doors to discrimination on orientation and gender-identity grounds, and the governor asked lawmakers to withdraw both bills on 13 June 2019. A 2017 religious freedom bill that would have let public businesses legally discriminate against LGBTQ people was vetoed by Rosselló in February 2018.

The care ban's severity is measured against the rest of the United States: the report documenting Ley 63 de 2025 places it as the most restrictive such law in any United States jurisdiction, and Amnesty International's Puerto Rico reporting records its signing in July 2025 alongside the wider regional pattern of restrictions on gender-affirming health care.
localsOnly:
House Bill 488, signed 29 May 2013, extended domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity, giving residents a local remedy that does not depend on the employment-only anti-discrimination statute.

Residents under 21 lose access to gender-affirming care entirely, and public funding for that care is barred, so the ban is not a visitor-specific restriction but the island's standing rule for its own trans young people. Local medical and counselling bodies, the Bar Association and the LGBTQ+ Federation opposed the measure, and the Federation has announced a court challenge; the ACLU of Puerto Rico has campaigned against it since before signature.

Conversion therapy for minors remains unregulated by statute after Senate Bill 1000 failed in the House in 2019, and the religious-freedom bills of 2017 and 2019 were vetoed and withdrawn respectively rather than enacted.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Article 3's definition of banned chemical and surgical practice can be applied against a patient rather than a provider, and whether the conflict between that definition and Article 4's operative clause has been litigated, remain unresolved in the sources; no test case had tested the question at the time of writing.

No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections policy on transgender inmate housing, dedicated unit or court ruling was located, so the federal Bureau of Prisons practice under Executive Order 14168 is the only sourced account of custody conditions on the island.

The scope of the mandated Education and Health department campaigns on the risks of trans-affirming care, and any guidance issued to schools or hospitals under them, is not documented in the available material.
